title: Tamagoyaki
subtitle: rolled sweet Japanese omelette
excerpt: Tamagoyaki is a Japanese rolled omelette sweetened with mirin and sugar. Thin layers of egg are cooked in a rectangular pan and rolled into a log as each layer sets. Serves 4 as a side dish or bento item.
sourceNotes: Tamagoyaki is a foundational element of Japanese bento culture. It is also a standard topping at sushi restaurants. The skill of rolling it cleanly is considered a mark of a good cook and is tested in traditional Japanese cookery training.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made up to 4 hours ahead. Wrap in cling film while warm and slice just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Japanese rolled omelette made by cooking thin layers of egg in a rectangular tamagoyaki pan and rolling each layer into the previous one to create a compact log.
Sweet Japanese rice wine. In tamagoyaki it provides both sweetness and a subtle shine to the finished omelette.

content.text: and sugar giving the egg a mild sweetness. A rectangular tamagoyaki pan is traditional but a small round frying pan works well. The rolling technique improves quickly with practice. Serves 4.
The egg mixture should not be foamy. Stir gently with chopsticks rather than whisking vigorously so you do not add air bubbles that would disrupt the texture.
Crack the eggs into a jug. Add the mirin, sugar and soy sauce. Stir gently with chopsticks to combine without creating foam. Pass through a sieve if the mixture is not smooth.
Heat a tamagoyaki pan or small frying pan over medium heat. Brush very lightly with oil using a folded piece of kitchen paper.

Pour in about one third of the egg mixture. Tilt the pan so it covers the base in a thin layer. When the edge starts to set but the centre is still slightly wet, use a spatula to roll the egg from one end to the other into a log. Push the log to the far edge of the pan.

Brush the exposed pan with a little more oil. Pour in another third of the egg mixture, lifting the existing log to let the new egg flow underneath. When mostly set, roll the first log back over the new layer, incorporating it. Push back to the far edge again. Repeat with the remaining egg.
Remove the tamagoyaki from the pan and shape into a neat log by rolling it in a bamboo mat or cling film and pressing gently. Rest for 5 minutes then slice into rounds and serve.

attrs.cause: Egg was left too long before rolling so it became too firm
attrs.fix: Roll when the egg is 80% set with the centre still slightly wet. It will finish cooking as you roll.

attrs.cause: Not enough overlap between each layer when rolling, or the pan was not oiled between layers
attrs.fix: Brush oil before each pour. Make sure to let new egg flow under the existing roll so the layers bond.

attrs.symptom: Egg is browned on the outside
attrs.fix: Keep the heat at medium throughout. Tamagoyaki should be pale yellow with no browning.

content.text: Tamagoyaki appears in almost every Japanese bento box. It is also served as a nigiri sushi topping. Sushi chefs use it to test new cooks: the quality of the tamagoyaki reflects the care of the person who made it. At home, most families have a tamagoyaki pan which is used most mornings. Once the rolling technique is in your muscle memory, it takes under 5 minutes.
